Q: Any recourse with applying a functional based index to multiple situations? A:

Your index

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX unique_active_order
    ON orders (CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END);

guarantees there to exist only one active order per customer. Moreover, it will probably only point to rather few rows in the table data, as of all of a customer's orders only one will be open.

A query to get the open orders using the index would have to include CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END and should hence be

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL;

Including tasks for these open orders:

WITH open_orders AS 
(
  SELECT *
  FROM orders
  WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT <whatever subset>
FROM open_orders oo
LEFT OUTER JOIN task t ON t.order_id = oo.id;

Your index

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX unique_active_order ON orders (CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END);

guanrantees that there is only one active order per customer. Moreover, it will probably only point to rather few rows in the table data, as of all of a customer's orders only one will be open.

A query to get the open orders using the index would have to include CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END and should hence be

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL;

Including tasks for these open orders:

WITH open_orders AS 
(
  SELECT *
  FROM orders
  WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT <whatever subset>
FROM open_orders oo
LEFT OUTER JOIN task t ON t.order_id = oo.id;

This case is a very special one. The index's main purpose is to guarantee a uniqueness that common indexes and constraints cannot. But it also happens to contain a small particular subset of rows from the table that you often want to deal with in your queries, so you want to force the DBMS to consider this index in these queries. This is the exact opposite of the normal scenario. Generally, we want to have our queries as readable as possible and we write them accordingly. We don't want to be forced to think about possible indexes and alter our queries to match them. SQL is a declarative language where it shouldn't even matter how we write a query. The obvious query to get the open orders is

SELECT *
FROM orders
WHERE end_ts IS NULL;

And this is precisely how we would want to write it. Only, despite Oracle's optimizer being very good, it is not yet good enough to see that it could easily use our index here, as it contains exactly the rows the query requires. Now we are in a fix. We want our query as readable as possible, but we aso want it to be fast. We know Oracle should use the index. Oracle does not. So one solution is to replace WHERE end_ts IS NULL with the less readable WHERE CASE end_ts IS NULL THEN customer_id END IS NOT NULL, and we should put a comment in or above the query to explain why we are doing this. This can be considered a workaround for the time being until the optimizer is capable of detecting such situations itself.

The normal use of indexes is this: We write our queries as readable as possible and then provide appropriate indexes matching these queries. Sometimes, as Oracle establishes primary key constraints by means of a unique index, the indexes we want for our queries already exist. If not, we provide them ourselves. Having to modify a query to force the DBMS to consider an index really is an exception, and fortunately very rare at that.

Q: Kamailio Unable to Allocate Media Ports with rtpengine (Failed to Get Consecutive Ports) A:

The problem is setting interface two times in the configuration file, likely the second value is used, which probably is the public/advertised address, not local network interface address, and socket bind fails for it.

From the RTPEngine manual:

To configure multiple interfaces using the command-line options, simply present multiple -i or --interface options. When using the config file, only use a single interface line, but specify multiple values separated by semicolons (e.g. interface = internal/12.23.34.45;external/23.34.45.54).

Q: I can't get how to calculate DeltaTime in SDL3 A:

SDL_GetPerformanceCounter returns a counter value, not a time.

The counter values are only meaningful relative to each other. Differences between values can be converted to times by using SDL_GetPerformanceFrequency().

SDL_GetPerformanceFrequency returns the number of counts per second for the host platform.

last = SDL_GetPerformanceCounter(); gets the counter value at the start of the render loop, and now = SDL_GetPerformanceCounter(); gets the counter value just before calculating deltaTime. now - last is the number of counts (or ticks) that have passed in the counter so far in the current iteration of the render loop, and this "delta count" value is divided by the number of counts per second to calculate the value of deltaTime in seconds.

Q: Spring Boot cannot find table in Docker database A:

I found this after a few more google tries ....

To connect your Spring Boot 3.1.4 application to an existing, running database container without overriding or wiping its current data, you need to manage how Spring Boot's new spring-boot-docker-compose module interacts with your container infrastructure. [1]

The Core Strategy

By default, Spring Boot 3.1+ attempts to run docker compose up at launch and docker compose stop upon shutdown. To safely connect to your existing data, you must configure the module to ignore lifecycle management and define your database as an external, reusable service. [1]

Step 1: Configure the docker-compose.yml

You must use specific Docker Compose labels so Spring Boot 3.1 knows the database is managed externally. [1, 2]

yaml

version: '3.8'

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:15 # Use your exact DB image type (e.g., mysql, mariadb, etc.)
    container_name: my_existing_db
    ports:
      - "5432:5432"
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_USER=myuser
      - POSTGRES_DB=mydatabase
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret
    labels:
      # CRITICAL: Tells Spring Boot NOT to stop or kill this container on shutdown
      org.springframework.boot.docker.compose.lifecycle.management: "none"
      # Tells Spring Boot to skip calling "docker compose up" if it's already there
      org.springframework.boot.readiness-check.skip: "true"

Step 2: Configure application.properties or application.yml

Tell Spring Boot exactly what to do when it scans your Docker environment. You can control its global behavior with these specific lifecycle keys:

properties

# Tells Spring Boot to connect to running containers, but do not start/stop them
spring.docker.compose.lifecycle-management=start-only

# Ensure Hibernate does not recreate tables and wipe existing data
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate

(Note: Use spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none or validate so your existing database schemas and rows are preserved). [1]

Step 3: Handle External Networks (If applicable)

If your existing database was started outside of this specific docker-compose project, it resides on a different Docker network. Your Spring Boot app won't see it unless they share a network bridge. [1]

Step 3: Handle External Networks (If applicable)

If your existing database was started outside of this specific docker-compose project, it resides on a different Docker network. Your Spring Boot app won't see it unless they share a network bridge. [1]

Update your docker-compose.yml to attach to that existing network: [1]

yaml

services:
  my-spring-app:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
    networks:
      - database_network

networks:
  database_network:
    external: true # Tells Docker to use your already existing network

What Spring Boot 3.1 Does Automatically

Once these configurations are established, the spring-boot-docker-compose module uses Service Connections via ConnectionDetails. It will: [1, 2]

  • Detect the already running my_existing_db container.

  • Extract the username, password, and port from the compose file.

  • Connect your app seamlessly without you needing to hardcode JDBC URLs in application.properties. [1, 2]

To proceed smoothly, could you share which database you are using (e.g., PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle) and whether your app will run inside a container or directly from your local IDE? I can tailor the network definitions for your exact setup. [1, 2, 3, 4]

Q: EPPlus library columns aligment in C# A:

In EPPlus you align columns by setting the HorizontalAlignment (VerticalAlignment) on the column’s Style, just like you would on a cell range.
For example:

worksheet.Column(2).Style.HorizontalAlignment = ExcelHorizontalAlignment.Center; worksheet.Column(2).Style.VerticalAlignment = ExcelVerticalAlignment.Center;
